entry: Religious, ideological, or philosophical beliefs based on [[Satan]]. Self-identified Satanism is a relatively modern phenomenon, largely attributed to the 1966 founding of the Church of Satan in the United States by [[Anton LaVey]]. That group is atheistic and does not believe in a supernatural Satan. Accusations of "devil worship" have recurred throughout Christian history. During the [[Middle Ages]], the [[Inquisition]] led by the [[Catholic Church]] alleged that heretical sects such as the Knights Templar performed secret Satanic rituals. In the early modern period, belief in a Satanic conspiracy of witches led to the trials and executions of tens of thousands of alleged witches, peaking between 1560 and 1630. Since the 19th century, small groups have identified as Satanist. Nontheistic Satanists regard Satan as a symbol of human traits, while theistic Satanists venerate Satan as a supernatural deity. Contemporary religious Satanism is predominantly American.

Ancient [[India|Indian]] dynasty that ruled the [[Deccan Plateau|Deccan]] from the late 2nd century BCE to the early 3rd century CE. Its territory mainly comprised present-day [[Andhra Pradesh]], [[Telangana]], and [[Maharashtra]], and at times extended into [[Gujarat]], Madhya Pradesh, and Karnataka. Its capitals included Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati (Dharanikota). The dynasty reached its zenith under Gautamiputra Satakarni and his successor Vasisthiputra Pulamavi, and by the early 3rd century CE the kingdom had fragmented into smaller states. In the post-Maurya era, the Satavahanas established peace in the Deccan and resisted foreign invaders, including the Saka (Western Satraps). They were early issuers of Indian state coinage bearing images of their rulers. They formed a cultural bridge between the [[Indo-Gangetic Plain]] and southern India, playing a vital role in trade and the transfer of ideas. Scholars debate the dynasty's origins and the meaning of its name.

Use of [[Satellite|satellites]] for navigation or geopositioning. A global navigation satellite system (GNSS) provides coverage for any user on Earth, including air, land, and sea. Four operational GNSS systems exist: the United States' [[Global Positioning System|Global Positioning System (GPS)]], [[Russia]]'s GLONASS, China's BeiDou, and the [[European Union]]'s Galileo. Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System and India's NavIC are regional systems. Satellite-based augmentation systems, such as WAAS and EGNOS, are designed to enhance the accuracy of the global systems. Receivers determine their location to within a few centimeters to meters using time signals transmitted by [[Radio|radio]] from satellites. The same signals allow receivers to calculate local time to high precision. Global coverage is generally achieved by a constellation of 18–30 medium Earth orbit satellites, at an altitude of about 20,000 kilometers (12,000 miles). Satellite navigation operates independently of telephone or internet reception.

Service that delivers television programming by relay from an orbiting [[Communications satellite|communications satellite]]. Viewers receive the signal with an outdoor parabolic dish and a low-noise block downconverter, and a receiver decodes the program for the television set. It is often the only television service available in remote areas without terrestrial or [[Cable television|cable]] service. Some channels are free-to-air, others are [[Encryption|encrypted]], and pay television requires a monthly subscription. Modern systems use digital signals on the X band (8–12 GHz) or Ku band (12–18 GHz), requiring a dish less than a meter in diameter. The first systems, called television receive-only, used weaker analog C-band (4–8 GHz) signals and needed dishes 2–3 meters across, making them expensive and unpopular. Satellites carrying television are usually in [[Geostationary orbit|geostationary orbit]], about 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the [[Equator]], so dishes can stay aimed at one point. Digital broadcasting also made high-definition television practical.

Genre of the visual, literary, and performing arts that holds vices, follies, and abuses up to ridicule. Satire is usually meant to be humorous, but its greater purpose is often constructive social criticism aimed at improving individuals, corporations, governments, or society. A prominent feature is strong irony or sarcasm, though [[Parody]], burlesque, exaggeration, and double entendre are also common. Laughter is not essential, and some satire is not meant to be funny at all. The word derives from the [[Latin]] *satura*, a mixed dish or medley, rather than from the mythological [[Satyr|satyr]]. Its origin is often traced to the Old Comedy of [[Aristophanes]] in ancient Greece. In *A Modest Proposal* (1729), [[Jonathan Swift]] hyperbolically advocated eating Irish children to expose neglect during a famine.

Pseudonym used by the presumed creator or creators of [[Bitcoin]]. Nakamoto published Bitcoin's white paper in October 2008, released the original software in January 2009, and devised the first [[Blockchain|blockchain]] database. Nakamoto used a Japanese name and listed Japan as residence, though many have speculated that the author is a British software and cryptography expert. Nakamoto's true identity remains unknown. Nakamoto was active in development until December 2010. The wallet attributed to Nakamoto has been untouched since 2010 and is estimated to hold 1.1 million bitcoins.

American late-night live sketch comedy and variety show on [[NBC]], created by [[Lorne Michaels]]. It premiered on October 11, 1975, hosted by [[George Carlin]], under the title *NBC's Saturday Night*. Each episode features a celebrity host and a musical guest and is broadcast live before a studio audience in [[New York City|New York]]. Former cast members include [[John Belushi]], [[Gilda Radner]], and [[Tina Fey]]. The show has aired 1,014 episodes, one of the longest-running network television programs in the United States. Sketches have inspired films such as *The Blues Brothers* (1980) and *Wayne's World* (1992).

Painting by Spanish artist [[Francisco Goya]], one of fourteen so-called Black Paintings. Goya painted it directly on the walls of his house, the Quinta del Sordo near [[Madrid]], between 1820 and 1823. It was transferred to canvas after his death and now hangs in the [[Museo del Prado]]. The painting is traditionally read as the [[Greek mythology|Greek myth]] of Cronus, whom the Romans called Saturn, eating one of his children out of fear of a prophecy. Goya did not provide a title or notes, so its interpretation is disputed.

Retired American super heavy-lift launch vehicle developed by [[NASA]] for the [[Apollo program]]. Thirteen Saturn V rockets were launched from 1967 to 1973, all from [[Kennedy Space Center]] Launch Complex 39. Nine of them launched 24 astronauts toward the Moon, from Apollo 8 to Apollo 17, and the final launch carried [[Skylab]], the first American space station. The Saturn V was the first launch vehicle to carry humans beyond low Earth orbit and holds the record for the largest payload capacity to low Earth orbit, at 140,000 kg (310,000 lb). It had three liquid-fueled stages. Its first stage used five F-1 engines, which remain the most powerful single-chamber liquid-fueled engines ever built. The design was led technically by [[Wernher von Braun]], one of the scientists relocated from Nazi Germany, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in [[Huntsville, Alabama]].

Persistent, roughly hexagonal cloud pattern around the north pole of [[Saturn]]. Voyager flybys in 1981 recorded it, and Cassini–Huygens revisited it in 2006. Its sides are about 14,500 kilometers long. It may be a [[Jet stream|jet stream]] of gases moving at 320 kilometers per hour. It rotates with a period of 10h 39m 24s, the same as Saturn's radio emissions. The south pole has no hexagon, but a decagon-shaped wave pattern that formed around 2023. One hypothesis holds that the hexagon forms where wind speed changes steeply with latitude, a shape reproduced in laboratory tanks of rotating liquid.

Indian film director, screenwriter, and author, widely considered one of the greatest and most influential directors in the history of cinema. Ray was born in Calcutta to the author Sukumar Ray and Suprabha Ray. He began as a commercial artist before he was drawn into independent filmmaking after meeting [[Jean Renoir]] and seeing Vittorio De Sica's Italian neorealist *Bicycle Thieves* during a visit to London. His debut, *Pather Panchali* (1955), won eleven international prizes, including the inaugural Best Human Document award at the 1956 [[Cannes Film Festival]]. Its sequels, *Aparajito* and *Apur Sansar*, completed *The Apu Trilogy*. Ray directed 36 films and wrote novels and short stories, including the sleuth Feluda. He received a record 37 Indian National Film Awards and an Academy Honorary Award in 1992. The Government of India honored him with the Bharat Ratna, its highest civilian award, in 1992.

Indian theoretical physicist and mathematician. Bose is best known for his work on [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] in the early 1920s, which laid the foundation for Bose–Einstein statistics and the theory of the [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]. The particles described by his statistics, [[Boson|bosons]], were named by [[Paul Dirac]]. Born in [[Kolkata|Calcutta]], Bose earned top marks at Presidency College and in 1916 became a research scholar at Calcutta University. He was a Fellow of the Royal Society, and in 1954 the Government of India awarded him the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian award. A [[Polymath|polymath]], he had interests in physics, mathematics, chemistry, biology, mineralogy, philosophy, arts, literature, and music. After independence, he served on many research and development committees in India.

Male nature spirit in [[Greek mythology]], with ears and a tail resembling those of a horse. Satyrs were companions of the god [[Dionysus]], known as lovers of wine, music, and dancing, and believed to inhabit woodlands, mountains, and pastures. In [[Classical Athens|classical Athens]], satyrs formed the chorus of the satyr play, a parody of tragedy known for bawdy humor. The only complete surviving satyr play is [[Euripides]]' *Cyclops*. The Romans identified them with native fauns. Since the [[Renaissance]] they have most often been shown with the legs and horns of goats.

Liquid, cream, or semi-solid food served on or used in preparing other foods. Most sauces are not eaten alone; they add flavor, texture, and visual appeal. The word comes from French, probably from post-classical Latin *salsa*, derived from the classical *salsus*, meaning salted. Possibly the oldest recorded European sauce is garum, a fish sauce used by the ancient Romans. The Aztecs are thought to have made one of the oldest sauces, hot sauce from [[Chili pepper|chili peppers]] and water, in roughly 7000 BCE. Sauces may be served cold, like [[Mayonnaise]], or cooked and served warm. Composed sauces, important in classical [[French cuisine]], are made in the kitchen, and the five mother sauces were refined by Georges Auguste Escoffier in his 1903 cookbook *Le Guide Culinaire*. In Asian cooking, sauces are often built into a dish, as in curries, or used as a [[Condiment|condiment]], such as [[Soy sauce|soy sauce]].

Majority state-owned [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and [[Natural gas|natural gas]] company of [[Saudi Arabia]]. Headquartered in Dhahran, it was the fourth-largest company in the world by revenue as of 2024. It holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, more than 270 billion barrels, and has the largest daily oil production of any oil-producing company. It operates the Ghawar Field, the world's largest onshore oil field,. Its shares began trading on the Saudi Exchange on December 11, 2019. In 2024 it was responsible for more CO2 emissions than any other entity, counting Scope 3 emissions from the oil it sells.

Canadian and American writer. Born in Lachine, Quebec, to Jewish parents who had emigrated from [[Saint Petersburg]], Russia, Bellow grew up in Chicago, the city that forms the backdrop of many of his novels. He received the [[Pulitzer Prize]] and the 1976 Nobel Prize in Literature, and he is the only writer to win the National Book Award for Fiction three times. His best-known works include *The Adventures of Augie March*, *Henderson the Rain King*, *Herzog*, *Mr. Sammler's Planet*, *Seize the Day*, *Humboldt's Gift*, and *Ravelstein*. The Swedish Nobel Committee praised the mixture of picaresque novel and subtle analysis of culture. [[Christopher Hitchens]] described Bellow's characters as striving to overcome not just ghetto conditions but also ghetto psychoses.

Heated room or building for dry or wet heat sessions, or an establishment with such facilities. Bathers sweat in high heat, and steam is produced when water is thrown on hot stones. The word is an ancient Finnish term for both the traditional Finnish bath and the bathhouse. The first Finnish smoke saunas (savusauna) were heated for six to eight hours by burning wood under a pile of stones called a kiuas, and could yield heat for up to 12 hours. After the [[Industrial Revolution]], saunas used wood-burning metal stoves with a chimney, and air temperatures in traditional Finnish saunas averaged 75–100 °C (167–212 °F), sometimes exceeding 110 °C (230 °F). Traditional [[Korea|Korean]] saunas, called hanjeungmak, are domed stone structures first mentioned in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty in the 15th century, when [[Sejong the Great]] promoted their health benefits.

Extinct clade of saurischian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] with very long necks and tails. Sauropods had small heads and four thick, pillar-like legs, and the group includes the largest animals ever to live on land. The name, coined by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878, means "lizard foot" in Greek. The oldest unequivocal sauropods date from the [[Jurassic|Early Jurassic]]. By the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago, they were widespread, especially diplodocids and brachiosaurids. By the Late Cretaceous the titanosaurs had replaced all other sauropods, with a near-global distribution, but like all other non-avian dinosaurs they died out in the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]]. Fossils have been found on every continent. Complete skeletons are extremely rare, and many of the largest species are known only from isolated bones.

Meat product usually made from ground meat, most often [[Pork|pork]], [[Beef|beef]], or [[Poultry|poultry]], with salt, spices, and other flavorings. Grains or breadcrumbs may be added as fillers or extenders. Sausages are usually formed in a casing, traditionally made from cleaned intestines and now often made from collagen, cellulose, or plastic. Sausage making is a traditional form of [[Food preservation|food preservation]], using curing, drying, smoking, or freezing, and some cured or smoked sausages can be stored without refrigeration. The word derives from Vulgar Latin *salsica*, from *salsicus*, meaning seasoned with salt. Sausages were already popular among the [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greeks]] and Romans, and [[Homer]] mentioned a blood sausage in the *Odyssey*. In the 21st century, vegetarian and vegan varieties made from plant ingredients have become much more widely available.

Mixed woodland-grassland [[Biome|biome]] and ecosystem in which trees are spaced so that the canopy does not close. The open canopy lets enough light reach the ground to support an unbroken layer of grasses. Savannas take four forms: savanna woodland, tree savanna, shrub savanna, and grass savanna. Despite their open look, savannas can have high tree densities; South American cerrado ranges from 800 to 3,300 trees per [[Hectare|hectare]], and Guinean savanna has 129 trees per hectare. Most rain falls in a single season. Savannas cover about 20% of [[Earth|Earth's]] land area and lie mostly in warm to hot climates, in [[Australia]], [[India]], South America, and Africa. Unlike the [[Prairie|prairies]] of North America and [[Steppe|steppes]] of Eurasia, they lack cold winters. The word comes from Spanish *sabana*, a loanword from Taíno meaning treeless grassland.

City and county seat of Chatham County, [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Founded on February 12, 1733, it was the capital of the colonial Province of Georgia and is the oldest city in the state. A strategic port during the [[American Revolution]] and the [[American Civil War]], it is today an industrial center and an important Atlantic seaport. The 2020 census recorded 147,780 residents. The downtown retains James Oglethorpe's original town plan, with 22 parklike squares, and its historic district is one of the largest National Historic Landmark Districts in the U.S. Savannah hosted sailing events for the 1996 Summer Olympics, held in [[Atlanta]].

1998 American war film directed by [[Steven Spielberg]] and written by Robert Rodat. Set in [[Normandy]] during [[World War II]], it follows a squad led by Captain John Miller ([[Tom Hanks]]) on a mission to find Private James Francis Ryan ([[Matt Damon]]), whose three brothers have been killed in action. The opening Omaha Beach battle cost $12 million to film over four weeks. The film earned $481.8 million, the second-highest-grossing film of 1998, and won many awards, including Golden Globe, Academy, and BAFTA awards. In 2014 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

[[Tool]] consisting of a tough blade, wire, or chain with a hard toothed edge, used to cut through material, most often [[Wood|wood]]. Saws began as serrated materials, and [[Iron|iron]] became the preferred blade material once people learned to use it. Many hand saws and mechanical saws exist, with several terms for toothed and abrasive types. The narrow channel a saw leaves is its kerf, a term that also refers to the wasted material turned into sawdust. Teeth are bent sideways, or set, so that the kerf is wider than the blade and the blade moves without binding. A ripsaw's tooth set resembles the angle of a [[Chisel|chisel]], so it tears the material apart, while a flush-cutting saw has no set on one side and can cut along a surface without scratching it.

Family of very large rays with a long, flattened snout lined with sharp transverse teeth. Sawfish are among the largest fish, with some species reaching about 7–7.6 meters (23–25 feet). They live in tropical and subtropical coastal seas and estuaries, and sometimes in freshwater rivers and lakes. They detect and capture fish and invertebrates with the [[Saw|saw]], and are generally harmless to humans, though they can inflict serious injuries when captured. Sawfish breed slowly, and females give birth to live young. All living species are [[Endangered species|critically endangered]]. Populations have declined drastically, and the remaining strongholds are in Northern Australia and [[Florida]]. Sawfish are hunted for their fins, used in shark fin soup, and for their teeth and rostrum, used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]]. The five living species are placed in two genera.

[[Germanic peoples|Germanic]] people of early medieval Old Saxony, in what is now northern Germany. The continental Saxons appeared as inland opponents of the [[Franks]] in the sixth century and were not politically united until the conflict that led to their defeat by [[Charlemagne]]. He conquered them after the Saxon Wars (772–804) and forced them to convert to Christianity. Saxony became a Carolingian stem duchy in 804. The first definite use of "Saxon" in written records describes coastal raiders who attacked the Roman Empire from north of the [[Rhine]], a sense similar to the later term Viking. These raiders included Frisians, Angles, and Jutes, as well as the [[Anglo-Saxons]] who became established in Britain. The name survives in [[Lower Saxony]], which includes most of the original duchy, and the Saxons' language evolved into Low German, the lingua franca of the [[Hanseatic League]].
